Guru Nanak. Fourteen sixty-nine to fifteen thirty-nine. The founding guru of Sikhism, a monotheistic religion emphasizing equality, community service, and devotion to God. Emerging in Punjab at a time of religious and social division, he created a tradition that bridges Hindu and Islamic elements while asserting its own distinctive spiritual path. Guru Nanak was born in Dera Baba Nanak in what is now Pakistan, during a period of tension between Hindu and Muslim communities in the Punjab region. He taught Ik Onkar, There is One God, emphasizing a formless, transcendent divinity accessible to all people regardless of caste, creed, or gender—revolutionary ideas for his time. His core message centered on Nam Simran, remembrance of God's name, Kirat Karna, honest living, and Vand Chhakna, sharing with others, the foundation of Sikh ethical practice. He rejected the ritualism, caste hierarchy, and claims of priestly authority in both Hinduism and Islam, advocating direct personal connection to the divine. Guru Nanak established the Langar, the communal kitchen, where all people—regardless of caste, religion, or social status—eat together as equals, embodying his egalitarian principles. He compiled the Guru Granth Sahib, the sacred scripture of Sikhism, which includes his own hymns and poetry alongside compositions from other saints and spiritual teachers. Sikhism preserves his legacy through ten successive Gurus, with the final Guru, Guru Granth Sahib, being the holy book itself that serves as the eternal guide for the faith. His life was devoted to spiritual practice, social reform, and traveling throughout Asia preaching his message of monotheism and human equality.
